notes:
I've written notes for all 22 verses. A few gaps first: I couldn't reach bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org notes, the Wesley site, oca.org or any Catholic or Orthodox commentary on this chapter, and I found nothing from prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers. Those sections are left out or kept thin.

On tradition labels: only StudyLight labels a writer's tradition (Gill as a Calvinist Baptist). The other labels (Clarke as Methodist, Henry as Presbyterian, the Pulpit Commentary as Anglican) are my own, not stated on the pages.

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- Guzik: Job widens his own frailty into a statement about everyone. Human days are short and often full of trouble. Having mentioned the idea of the frailty of men in general and his own frailty in particular, Job here expands on the idea. He considers that the days of man on this earth are short and often full of trouble. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-14/)
- Gill: "born of a woman" points to human weakness, not mainly to sin, since sin is the subject of v. 4. Job mainly means himself and uses his frailty to ask God for pity. This verse is a description of all mankind, yet Job chiefly designs himself, improving his frailty into an argument with God for pity and mercy. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/14-1.html)
- Pulpit Commentary: Job sees "born of a woman" as the source of man's built-in weakness, and the Hebrew reads literally "short of days."  (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-14.html)

**v. 2**
- Pulpit: the flower is one of the Bible's most common pictures, and Eastern flowers rarely last much more than a day. The fleeing shadow is probably a cloud's shadow racing over the ground. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-14.html)
- Guzik: the shadow picture also leads Job to wonder whether life simply stops at death. Job also speculated on what happened to man after this fading, shadow-like life; considering that perhaps it does not continue. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-14/)

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: Job doesn't doubt that God notices people. He is amazed that God would bother to judge and punish so weak a creature. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-14.html)
- Guzik: Job turns his thoughts into a prayer for his own case, asking God to look on him with mercy. Job here applied his previous thoughts on the fleeting and frail nature of humanity to prayer over his own situation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-14/)

**v. 4: a real disagreement (original sin or human weakness?)**
- Guzik: Job fears God wants a perfect cleanness he can never reach. If God demands perfect cleanness before He will relieve Job's affliction, then Job knew he could never meet that standard. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-14/)
- Clarke (Methodist): The text refers to man's original and corrupt nature. Every man that is born into the world comes into it in a corrupt or sinful state. This is called original sin; and is derived from fallen Adam. Only God can save from it. (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/job/14-4.html)
- Gill (Calvinist Baptist): no one sinless can come from sinful parents. Christ is the one exception, born of the Virgin by the Holy Spirit. Only God can make someone clean, by Christ's blood. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/14-4.htm)
- Matthew Henry (Presbyterian): our corruption comes with our nature from our parents. Here is a clear proof that Job understood and believed the doctrine of original sin. He seems to have intended it as a plea, why the Lord should not deal with him according to his own works, but according to His mercy and grace. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/14-4.htm)
- Spurgeon (Baptist) preached a sermon on this verse. He defends the doctrine against "new-fangled" teaching and says God must work the change by grace. Whatever the new-fangled teaching may say about the old-fashioned doctrine that we are shapen in iniquity, and conceived in sin, that doctrine is true. (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/out-of-nothing-comes-nothing)
- Pulpit Commentary (Anglican) disagrees in its main notes. It is scarcely true to say that "the fact of original sin is thus distinctly recognized". Original uncleanness and infirmity are recognized; but the uncleanness is material, and removable by material expiation. Its sermon section, however, says the verse may express the doctrine of inherited corruption. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-14.html)
- Coffman goes along with the Pulpit's main note: This passage does not teach, as some have asserted that, "Anyone born of woman is born in sin." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/14-4.html)
- Constable reads it as: "Who can without God's provision of grace make an unclean person clean?" (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/14-4.html)
- Other readings:
  - The Aramaic paraphrase (the Targum) and Jerome's Latin make the answer "God alone." Barnes calls this manifestly a departure from the sense of the passage. Jerome, however, has adopted nearly the same translation. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/14-4.htm)
  - The Catholic Douay-Rheims has: Who can make him clean that is conceived of unclean seed? is it not thou who only art? (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nrs/job/14-4.html)

**v. 5**
- Pulpit: God has fixed and knows the length of each life. The three phrases all say the same thing. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-14.html)
- Constable: God has indeed determined the life span of every individual. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/14-4.html)

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: "look away" means "stop watching him so closely." A hired worker is glad when the day's work ends, and so man is glad when life ends. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-14.html)
- Guzik: Job pictures God fencing man in, so it would be better if God just looked away and let the sufferer rest. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-14/)

**vv. 7–9**
- Pulpit: a cut stump, or even a dead one, can send up new shoots if it gets water. It cites Herodotus, Pliny and the traveller Shaw on how trees grow back. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-14.html)
- Guzik: there is a sort of resurrection in the world of trees and plants; new life can sprout out of an old stump. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-14/)

**v. 10**
- Pulpit: the word for "man" here (*geber*) means the strong man; even he perishes. "Where is he?" admits Job couldn't say what Sheol, the place of the dead, was like. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-14.html)
- Barnes: unlike a stump, a dead man has no seed of new life left in him. He adds that this refers wholly to his living again on the earth, and not to the question about his future existence. (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/job/14-10.html)
- Guzik: to Job it seemed unfair. Why should a tree have a better hope of resurrection than a man? (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-14/)

**v. 11**
- Clarke: water evaporates and rivers dry up, yet the sea stays full. In the same way one person disappears but the human race goes on. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-14.html)
- Pulpit: Job may have known seas and rivers that really did dry up in Mesopotamia. Its sermon section says man's true picture is not the trees, but the streams and the lakes. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-14.html)

**v. 12: did Job know about the resurrection?**
- Pulpit: This isn't a flat denial of a final resurrection. Job describes the world as he sees it. The phrase "until the heavens are no more" happens to match the New Testament timing, and calling death "sleep" carries a glimmer of hope of waking. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-14.html)
- Matthew Henry: man returns to life when the heavens are no more. The resurrection of the dead was doubtless an article of Job's creed. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_014.cfm)
- Guzik (Calvary Chapel): We can simply say that Job was wrong in his understanding of the afterlife. God later corrects him (Job 38:2, 17). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-14/)
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel): The things that Job are saying about death cannot be taken for doctrinal truth. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/14-14.html)
- Constable: He believed in life after death (Job 14:13) but he did not know that there would be bodily resurrection from Sheol. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/14-14.html)

**v. 13**
- Pulpit: Sheol here means the place of departed spirits. Job wants God to shelter him there for a set time and then remember him. The scholar Schultens thought Job wished to go down alive. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-14.html)
- Barnes: probably a wish for a safe hiding place. But whether Job meant the grave, or the place of departed spirits, cannot be determined, and is not material. He also sees the secret hope of some future life - though remote. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/14-13.html; https://www.studylight.org/bible/tgl/ceb/job/14-13.html)
- Clarke: "hide me in the grave" refers to the body, and "keep me secret" refers to the spirit. (https://www.studylight.org/bible/tgl/ceb/job/14-13.html)
- BibleHub Study Bible: Job's closing plea, "remember me," looks ahead to resurrection and a restored relationship with God. (https://biblehub.com/job/14-13.htm)
- Catholic translation: the Douay-Rheims reads that thou mayest protect me in hell, using "hell" for the place of the dead. (https://biblehub.com/job/14-13.htm)

**v. 14: the chapter's main debate**
- Expected answer "No":
  - Pulpit: The question is clearly intended to be answered in the negative. It is not a dispassionate inquiry, but an expression of hopelessness. It translates "change" as "renewal," whose exact sense is unclear. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-14.html)
  - Barnes: the question is a strong way of saying no, he won't live again on earth. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/14-14.html)
- Expected answer "Yes":
  - Coffman: The answer that the scholars generally give here is a decided NO; but we reject that misunderstanding of the passage. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/14-14.html)
  - Clarke, on the Greek Septuagint: Here is no doubt, but a strong persuasion, of the certainty of the general resurrection. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/14-14.html)
- Both "No" and "Yes":
  - Spurgeon: no, not to this life, so the sinner has no second chance. Yes, yes, that he shall. He does not die like a dog; he shall live again; not here, but in another and a better or a more terrible land. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/14-14.html)
  - Gill: not in this world, but yes at the general resurrection. The "change" is either death or the resurrection, and Job resolves to wait patiently. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/14-14.html)
  - Matthew Henry: the "change" is either the resurrection, which makes the question an expression of wonder, or death. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_014.cfm)
  - Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: no for this present world, yes for a future resurrection, though Job probably didn't see the second clearly. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/14-1.html)
- Guzik, quoting the scholar Andersen: Job's readiness to die in faith turns Sheol into a temporary hiding place. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-14/)
- Maclaren pictures the renewed life as like the 'release' of a sentry who had long stood on guard. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/job/jobs-question-jesus-answer.cfm)
- Jewish rendering: Clarke reports that the Aramaic paraphrase reads If a wicked man die, can he ever live again? (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-14.html)
- On critical scholars: Coffman cites Andersen, who says many scholars deny any resurrection hope here only because of "Their a priori belief that the idea of a resurrection arose quite late in Israel's thought." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/14-16.html)

**v. 15**
- Pulpit reads it as a wish ("you *would* call"). Job assumes God must love what he has made. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-14.html)
- Guzik: Job hopes for a restored relationship with God after death, and quotes Clarke that God longs for the dead to rise. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-14/)
- Coffman: the wording is firm. God *will* call and Job *will* answer. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/14-14.html)

**vv. 16–17: forgiveness or a record of sin?**
- The BSB reads these verses hopefully (God would not keep track of sin). The Pulpit reads v. 16 as "but now," setting Job's real situation against his wish. God watches his every step, and the "sealed bag" is a secure record of every sin, kept ready to be used against him. Some older scholars read v. 17 as God adding to his sins. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-14.html)
- Guzik's quoted note: Job's sins were counted, and sealed so that none could be lost. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-14/)
- Matthew Henry: Job admits he deserves his suffering. God seals up the sins of the unrepentant, but the sins of his people he blots out as a cloud. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_014.cfm)

**vv. 18–19**
- Pulpit: a collapsing mountain, a dislodged rock, worn stones and washed-out soil are four pictures of how God ruins a prosperous man's hopes. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-14.html)
- Guzik: the poem slides back into despair, but quoting Andersen he says vv. 14–17 are still the high point of the speech, and reaffirm the faith already expressed in chapter 13. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-14/)

**v. 20**
- Gill: no one can resist God, or the disease and death he sends. "Changes his countenance" means the face changing in dying. He mentions Maimonides' reading that it refers to Adam being sent out of Eden. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/14-20.html)
- Pulpit: God keeps pressing him down until he passes away to Sheol. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-14.html)

**vv. 21–22**
- Pulpit: in Sheol the dead don't know whether their sons rise or fall, a bleaker view than Aristotle's. Verse 22 means a suffering man can think only of his own pain. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-14.html)
- Guzik: Job's grief is real. He compares it to Jesus' cry "Why have You forsaken Me?" (Mark 15:34): the feelings were true even though a larger truth was hidden from Job. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-14/)
